summary: Vik Paruchuri presents Datalab's approach to building a high-impact AI company with a tiny team. Datalab grew 5x in revenue since January to 7-figure ARR, with customers including tier 1 AI labs, universities, Fortune 500 companies, and AI startups like Gamma. The team consists of four people building popular open-source repos (Surya, Marker) and training custom document intelligence models. Vik's philosophy stems from two sources: his experience at Data Quest, where two rounds of layoffs (30 to 15 to 7) paradoxically improved productivity and happiness, and Jeremy Howard's approach at Answer AI of hiring fewer than 15 generalists who can work across the entire stack. He identifies four reasons large teams underperform: specialists can't flex across problems, remote work requires heavy syncing, middle management creates meeting overload, and senior people get tied down managing juniors. Datalab operates with three core overlapping roles—research engineer, full-stack engineer, and go-to-market—where everyone talks to customers and builds product. Politics are the death of small teams; the company seeks people with minimal ego who care about the work, their colleagues, and customers. Vik pays top-of-market salary, arguing startups that raise $20M should hire fewer people at higher pay rather than more people at $150-200K. He emphasizes patience in hiring—his worst hires came from urgency, his best from waiting for the right generalist even without an immediate role. To scale productivity rather than headcount, he recommends raising salary bands, investing in compute (64 GPUs vs 8), and adopting AI tools. The three-step interview process consists of a peer-level chat, a paid 10-hour project ($1,000), and a culture-fit review, with approximately 40% of interviewed candidates hired. Candidates are sourced through open-source work and Twitter. In Q&A, Vik notes that cutting features during layoffs forced ruthless prioritization, and that changing ossified large-company culture is impractical—better to start a new company and build something better.

sections.title: Introduction and Datalab Overview
sections.summary: Vik introduces himself as CEO of Datalab, presenting on achieving 40K GitHub stars, 7-figure ARR, and state-of-the-art models with a team of three. He left AI research, started a company, raised a seed round, and has grown revenue 5x since January with customers including tier 1 AI labs, universities, Fortune 500, and AI startups like Gamma.

sections.title: Data Quest Lessons and the Productivity Paradox
sections.summary: Vik describes his previous company Data Quest, which scaled to 30 people and $4M ARR bootstrapped during COVID, then underwent two layoff rounds (30 to 15 to 7). Surprisingly, productivity and happiness increased after both layoffs. He hypothesizes four causes: specialists can't flex, remote work requires heavy syncing, middle management creates meeting overload, and senior people get tied down managing juniors.

sections.title: Jeremy Howard's Philosophy and Prerequisites
sections.summary: Vik describes Jeremy Howard's approach at Answer AI: hire fewer than 15 generalists who understand all aspects of the company, fill edges with AI and internal tooling, and use simple boring tech. Prerequisites include a high cultural bar, high trust, and customer focus across all roles.

sections.title: Surya OCR 3: End-to-End Generalist Example
sections.summary: Vik details training Surya OCR 3, a 500M parameter model supporting 90 languages at 99% accuracy including math and character-level bounding boxes. Two people handled the entire process from customer conversations through architecture, data cleaning, training, inference, and product integration, avoiding context loss from team handoffs. AI handled low-leverage tasks while humans did higher-level work.

sections.title: Operationalizing the Small-Team Approach
sections.summary: Vik explains how to make this work: hire senior generalists (maturity, not years of experience), avoid over-complication (shell scripts over Kubernetes), work in person, reuse components aggressively, keep technology simple (server-rendered HTML, HTMX, Alpine, no React), and write clean modular code that AI can easily extend.

sections.title: Filling Edges with Models and Conclusion
sections.summary: Vik discusses replacing forward-deployed engineering teams with models that iterate on customer-specific document parsing. He acknowledges uncertainty about whether this will scale indefinitely, but emphasizes that saying no to traditional hiring is a choice that may trade short-term revenue efficiency for long-term company health.

sections.title: Team Roles, Hiring Philosophy, and Scaling Productivity
sections.summary: Vik describes three core overlapping roles at Datalab—research engineer, full-stack engineer, and go-to-market—where everyone talks to customers and builds product. Politics are the death of small teams; he seeks people with minimal ego who care about the work, colleagues, and customers. He pays top-of-market salary, arguing startups that raise $20M should hire fewer people at higher pay rather than more at $150-200K. He emphasizes meaningful work, screening for low ego and GSD, patience in hiring, and scaling productivity not headcount via higher salary bands, more compute, and AI tools.

sections.title: Q&A: Prioritization, Culture Change, Sourcing, and Interviews
sections.summary: In Q&A, Vik explains that during Data Quest layoffs they cut less relevant features, noting that large teams create unnecessary work while tiny teams force ruthless prioritization. On changing ossified large-company culture, he says it's impractical—better to start a new company. On sourcing, he uses open-source work and Twitter. He describes a three-step interview process: a peer-level problem-solving chat, a paid 10-hour project ($1,000), and a culture-fit review, with approximately 40% of interviewed candidates hired.
